title: The Building That Doesn't Exist
setting: a small radio station's call-in line

post.author: u/dead_air_dana
post.title: I screen calls for a tiny late-night radio show. At 2:13 AM a woman called to tell us we don't exist.

blocks.text: I produce *The Graveyard Line* on Hollow Pine 97.3, a station so small our studio used to be a dentist's office. One to four AM, I screen the calls. Truckers, nurses, insomniacs, and one man who only wants to talk about owls.

On Tuesday at 4 PM, Marcus, our volunteer computer guy, moved our website to a new server. The old one had hummed in the studio closet for ten years. He changed the address in our domain settings, watched the site load from the new machine, and switched the old one off. "Nobody will notice," he said.
At 2:13 AM a woman named Ivy called. She lives four streets from the studio.
"I listen through your website," she said. "Tonight it says you're not there. Not broken. Not there. *This site can't be reached.* Like nothing lives at that address anymore."
Our site was open on the studio PC while she said it. Stream playing. Song list updating.
I started asking every caller. Seven could see us. Two couldn't: Ivy, and a night nurse across town. Different streets, same internet company. Bramblewire.
The owl man used to fix phone lines. He had me read Ivy a command, letter by letter, that asks the internet for our address directly. Then I ran it on the studio PC.

02:21:00  ivy's laptop  hollowpinefm.com  44760  A  203.0.113.7
02:21:00  studio pc     hollowpinefm.com  83120  A  198.51.100.24
02:22:00  ivy's laptop  hollowpinefm.com  44700  A  203.0.113.7
Same name. Same minute. Two different addresses. Marcus texted back at 3 AM: 203.0.113.7 is the old server. The one in the closet. The one with no power.
And the number after our name on Ivy's lines kept shrinking. Sixty every minute. One every second. At 3:58 AM I had her run it one last time: 38940. It never once went up.
Her internet still sends her to the building we moved out of.
Ivy says she'll try again tonight. Marcus moves our stream server next month. What happens when that number hits zero? And how do we make sure nobody else gets sent to an empty building?

blocks.label: two_lookups.png

diagram.aria: Two lookups of hollowpinefm.com at 2:21 AM. Ivy's laptop asks Bramblewire's resolver, which answers 203.0.113.7 from its cache with 44,760 seconds left, so Ivy connects to the old server, which is switched off and never answers. The studio PC asks the studio's resolver, which asked after the move and answers 198.51.100.24, so the studio reaches the new server and the show plays.

blocks.caption: I drew this after the show. Same name, same minute, two answers. Bramblewire's resolver is still handing out the old address from its cache, with 44,760 seconds left on the clock.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: That number after your name on her lines. Divide it by 3600 and add it to 2:21 AM. Then ask Marcus what that setting was before he moved anything.

replies.author: u/dead_air_dana
replies.text: 12.43 hours. So 2:47 this afternoon? Marcus says he never touched "that setting." He doesn't even know what it's called.

comments.author: u/insomniac_ruth
comments.text: I'm on Bramblewire too. Couldn't see you either. Cleared my browser, restarted the router, nothing. Then I took my phone off the home internet and onto mobile data, and there you were. Same phone. Same room.

comments.author: u/packet_ghost
comments.text: Everyone's going to tell you to clear your cache. Ask yourself *whose* cache.

reply.prompt: Marcus moves the stream server next month. What should he do so nobody gets sent to an empty building again? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Tell listeners to clear their browser cache and restart their routers whenever the site moves.
options.part2: We read a notice on air every hour: clear your browser, restart your router. Ivy did all of it, twice. She left her router unplugged until morning. When she plugged it back in, the page still said we weren't there. Nothing in her house was holding the old address. Something outside it was.
options.senior: Clearing your own cache only helps if your resolver already has the new answer. Bramblewire's resolver held the old one for a full day, and no listener can reach into it.

options.text: Set the TTL to 60 seconds and leave it there for good. Every change will show up within a minute.
options.part2: Marcus set the TTL to 60 seconds and left it there. The stream move went smoothly, and most listeners followed us within a minute or two. But our DNS bill crept up, first visits felt a hair slower, and one listener's provider kept the old address for an hour anyway, because it never keeps anything for less than an hour.
options.senior: A short TTL makes changes show up fast, but every resolver has to ask again far more often: more queries, a bigger bill on paid DNS, and a slightly slower first visit. Some resolvers also enforce their own minimum. Go short around a change, then raise it.

options.text: A day or more before the move, lower the TTL to about 5 minutes and let the old one-day copies expire. Then move, keep the old server running until visits to it stop, and raise the TTL again.
options.part2: Two days before the move, Marcus lowered our TTL to 5 minutes. We waited out the old day-long copies, moved the stream on Thursday at 4 PM, and left the old server running. By 4:10, Ivy could hear us. So could everyone on Bramblewire. Visits to the old server dropped to almost nothing within the hour. Almost. Every night since, at 2:13 AM, something knocks on the old server and asks for the stream. It never looks up our name first. It already knows where we used to live.
options.senior: Lower the TTL at least one old TTL before the move, keep the old address answering until its traffic dies out, then raise the TTL. You can't flush the world's caches, but you can decide how long they keep you.

options.text: Call Bramblewire after the move and ask them to clear their resolver's cache.
options.part2: I called Bramblewire at 9 AM. After 40 minutes on hold, a tired man cleared their cache, and Ivy could hear us by lunch. Next month we moved the stream. This time it was Bramblewire, a phone company two towns over, and a college network I'd never heard of. I can't call every company on Earth. I tried.
options.senior: You can't flush caches you don't control, and there are resolvers everywhere: internet providers, offices, phones, public DNS services. The one thing you control is the TTL on your own record, and it only helps if you change it before the move.

sim.title: Look up the station yourself
sim.lede: You're Ivy. Each dot is one visit to hollowpinefm.com. The clock runs 600 times faster than real life, so an hour passes in 6 seconds. The dots move in slow motion: a real lookup takes milliseconds. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: visit twice and watch the second visit skip the phone book. Press Move, then visit: the dead server. Flush your own cache and visit again: still dead, because the resolver's copy is still counting down. Then reset, pick 60 seconds before your first visit, move, wait a moment, and visit.

explain.oneLine: Nothing vanished. Ivy's internet provider kept handing out the station's old address, because the record had told it to keep that answer for a whole day.

steps.title: Computers find each other by number.
steps.text: Every machine on the internet has an IP address, like 198.51.100.24. Think of it as a street address. People remember names like hollowpinefm.com instead, so something has to turn the name into the number. That something is DNS, the internet's phone book.

steps.title: Ivy's provider does the looking up for her.
steps.text: Ivy's laptop doesn't search the phone book itself. It asks a DNS resolver run by her internet provider, Bramblewire. If the resolver has no fresh answer saved, it asks around: a root server points it to the .com servers, a .com server points it to the station's own nameserver, and that nameserver answers with the station's A record, the address.

steps.title: Every answer comes with a timer.
steps.text: The record also carries a TTL, short for time to live: how many seconds anyone may keep a copy before asking again. The station's was 86400 seconds, one day. On Tuesday at 2:47 PM, Bramblewire's resolver looked up the station and saved 203.0.113.7 until 2:47 PM Wednesday. Each time Ivy visits, her browser and laptop save small copies of their own.

steps.title: Marcus changed the record at 4 PM. The copies never heard.
steps.text: The station's nameserver started answering 198.51.100.24 at once. But a resolver doesn't ask again until its timer runs out, so Bramblewire kept sending Ivy, the night nurse and every other customer to the old server, which was switched off. The number in her lines was that timer: 44,760 seconds at 2:21 AM is 12 hours and 26 minutes, which lands on 2:47 PM.

steps.title: "Propagation" is really caches expiring.
steps.text: People say a DNS change needs time to propagate, as if it travels. It doesn't. The new answer is ready the moment it's saved. The wait is every cache in the world letting its old copy expire, each on its own timer. The longest wait is the old TTL, which is why Ivy will hear the show again tonight.

diagram.aria: The lookup path. 1: Ivy's browser asks Bramblewire's resolver where hollowpinefm.com is. On a cache miss the resolver asks, in order, 2: a root server, 3: a .com TLD server and 4: the station's nameserver, whose A record now says 198.51.100.24 with a TTL of 86400 seconds. Bramblewire's cache still holds 203.0.113.7 until Wednesday 2:47 PM, so 5: Ivy connects to the old server, which is switched off. Everyone else lands on the new server.

explain.caption: Each arrow is a question, and each one gets an answer back. Steps 2 to 4 happen only on a cache miss. Bramblewire's resolver did them on Tuesday at 2:47 PM, got 203.0.113.7 with a one-day TTL, and won't ask again until 2:47 PM Wednesday. The record changed at 4 PM, but step 5 still sends Ivy to the old server.

fix.title: The fix: lower the TTL before the move, raise it after
fix.text: Engineers call a move like Marcus's a migration, and the DNS part has a standard routine. A day or more before the move (at least as long as the current TTL), lower the record's TTL to something short, such as 300 seconds. Then wait for the old one-day copies to expire everywhere. On moving day, every cache that obeys the timer holds your address for 5 minutes at most. Move, and keep the old server answering for a few days, either serving the site or passing visitors on to the new one, so anyone still holding the old address gets the show instead of silence. When traffic to the old server has stopped and the new one is solid, raise the TTL back to an hour or a day.

limits: Not every cache obeys the timer. Some resolvers set their own minimum or maximum TTL, some keep using an expired answer when they can't reach your nameserver (a standard feature called serve-stale), and some programs can be set to keep an address forever. That's why the old server stays up for a while.
You can't flush caches you don't control. Clearing your own browser or OS cache only helps if your resolver already has the new answer. Only Bramblewire could clear Bramblewire's resolver.

A short TTL costs something. Resolvers ask your nameserver far more often: more queries, a bigger bill on paid DNS services, and a slightly slower first visit each time a copy expires. That's why you raise it again after the move.

head: TTL on your record
Good
Bad
rows: Changes reach almost everyone within minutes. A bad change is quick to undo.
Many more queries. Slightly slower first visits. A bigger bill on paid DNS.
Fewer queries, faster repeat visits, cheaper. Saved copies keep working through a short nameserver hiccup.
A move or a mistake can take a full TTL to clear, and you can't speed it up afterwards.
Fast when it matters, cheap the rest of the time.
Takes planning: you have to remember a day before the move.

explain.seniorTake: DNS changes don't travel. Old answers expire. So the real deadline for a move is set a day earlier, by the TTL you chose long ago. Lower it before you need it, and keep the old building open until the last visitor has left.

realWorld.title: Facebook, October 4, 2021
realWorld.text: Facebook's problem was the opposite of Ivy's: the phone book itself became unreachable. During routine maintenance, a command meant to check the capacity of Facebook's backbone, the private network linking its data centers, accidentally took every one of those links down. A safety tool that should have stopped the command had a bug. Facebook's DNS servers are built to withdraw themselves when they can't reach the data centers, because that usually means the network is unhealthy. So they did: they stopped announcing their routes over BGP, the system networks use to tell each other which addresses they can reach. The nameservers were still running, but nobody could reach them, so the rest of the internet could no longer find Facebook's servers. To the world, facebook.com was a building that didn't exist.

realWorld.title: What resolvers saw that day
realWorld.text: Cloudflare runs the public resolver 1.1.1.1. On it, lookups for facebook.com started failing at around 15:50 UTC and worked again at 21:20 UTC, about five and a half hours later. Apps and people kept retrying, so Cloudflare's resolvers worldwide handled about 30 times more queries than usual. A name that can't be looked up is a site that can't be reached, however healthy the servers behind it are.

realWorld.title: AWS Route 53's own advice
realWorld.text: Route 53, Amazon's DNS service, describes the same trade-off in its documentation. A longer TTL means resolvers ask less often, which makes lookups faster and lowers your Route 53 bill, but a change such as a new IP address takes longer to take effect. For a name that's already in use, it recommends setting a shorter value first, such as 300 seconds, and raising it after you confirm the new settings are correct.

asked: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
You're moving a website to a new server. How do you keep it reachable while DNS catches up?
interview.answer: Walk the lookup in order: the browser's cache, the operating system's cache, then the resolver, which on a miss asks a root server, a TLD server and the authoritative nameserver, and caches the A record for its TTL. Then the move: lower the TTL at least one old TTL ahead, wait, switch, keep the old server answering until its traffic dies out, then raise the TTL. Name the limits before they ask: caches you don't control, programs that ignore TTLs, and the extra query load of a short TTL.

terms.def: A number that identifies a machine on the internet, like 198.51.100.24. It works like a street address: to reach a machine, you need its number.
The human-friendly name of a website, like hollowpinefm.com. People remember names and machines need numbers, so something has to translate.
The full web address you type, like https://hollowpinefm.com/schedule. The domain name is the part in the middle.
A computer that waits for requests and answers them. A web server sends you a site's pages. A nameserver answers DNS questions.
The app you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Firefox or Safari. It keeps a small cache of recent DNS answers.
The core software that runs a computer or phone, like Windows, macOS or Android. It keeps its own DNS cache, shared by every app on the machine.
Short for operating system. An OS cache is the DNS cache your laptop or phone keeps for all its apps.
Internet service provider: the company that connects your home or phone to the internet, like Bramblewire in this story. Most run a DNS resolver for their customers.
The box in your home that connects your devices to your internet provider.
Domain Name System: the internet's phone book. A worldwide system of servers that turns domain names into IP addresses.
The server that does the looking up for you. Your device asks it a name, and it answers from its cache or asks around, then hands back the address. Usually run by your ISP.
A DNS resolver anyone can use instead of their ISP's, such as Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8.
A server that holds DNS information and answers questions about it. Root servers, TLD servers and authoritative nameservers are all nameservers.
The first stop in a full lookup. It doesn't know any website's address. It only knows which servers look after each ending, like .com or .org.
Top-level domain: the last part of a name, like .com or .org. A TLD server knows which authoritative nameserver holds the records for each name under it.
The nameserver that holds a domain's official records, set by its owner. Every other answer out there is a cached copy of what it said.
One entry in a domain's DNS settings, such as which IP address the name points to. Each record has a type, a value and a TTL.
The DNS record that maps a name to an IP address. The A in the station's lookup lines means this kind of record.
Time to live: a number of seconds attached to every DNS answer, saying how long anyone may keep a copy before asking again. 86400 seconds is one day.
A saved copy of an answer, kept so you don't have to ask again. Fast, but it can go stale: it keeps the old answer until it expires.
Saved DNS answers. Your browser, your operating system and your resolver each keep one, and each copy expires on its own TTL timer.
When a fresh answer is already saved in a cache, so nobody else has to be asked.
When a cache has no fresh answer, so the question has to go further. For a resolver, that means a full lookup.
Finding the IP address for a name, like "what is the address of hollowpinefm.com?" It may be answered from a cache or by asking around.
One question sent to a DNS server. A full lookup takes several queries: one to a root server, one to a TLD server, one to the authoritative nameserver.
What a resolver does on a cache miss: it asks a root server, then a TLD server, then the authoritative nameserver, and saves the answer for its TTL.
To clear a cache on purpose, so the next request has to ask again. You can only flush caches you control.
What people call the wait after a DNS change. Nothing travels: the new answer is ready at once. The wait is old cached copies expiring.
Moving a system from one place to another, like a website from an old server to a new one.
Audio or video sent over the internet as it happens, so listeners can hear the show live in a browser.
A building full of servers, with its own power, cooling and network links.
A company's own high-speed network linking its data centers to each other and to the rest of the internet.
Border Gateway Protocol: how networks tell each other which IP addresses they can reach. If a network stops announcing a route, nobody can find the way there.
A standard resolver feature that keeps using an expired answer when the authoritative nameserver can't be reached, instead of failing.
Coordinated Universal Time, the clock engineers use so timestamps from around the world line up.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud. Companies rent servers, storage and services like Route 53 from it.
Amazon's DNS service, part of AWS. It runs authoritative nameservers for your domains and lets you edit their records and TTLs.
In Route 53, the container that holds one domain's DNS records.

atWork: Open Route 53 in your AWS account (or ask whoever runs your DNS) and pick a record your team depends on, such as the A record for your main website. Read its TTL. Work out how long a bad change to that record could keep sending users to the wrong place. Then write down what you would set it to a day before moving that server (300 seconds is a common choice), how long you would wait before the move, and who will raise it again afterwards. If you only have read access, the hosted zone's record list shows every TTL without changing anything.

recall.prompt: Ivy kept getting the old address for hours after the station changed its record. What decided how long?
options: How far Ivy lives from the station
The TTL on the station's DNS record
How busy the root servers were
recall.why: The TTL tells every resolver how long it may keep a copy. The station's was one day, so Bramblewire's resolver kept the old answer for up to a day after it last asked.

recall.prompt: Your internet provider's resolver still has an old address for a site. Which of these actually gets you to the new server?
options: Waiting for the resolver's copy to expire, or using a different resolver
Reloading the page over and over
recall.why: Your own caches aren't the problem: the resolver hands the old answer right back. Only its timer running out, or asking a different resolver (like a phone on mobile data), gets a fresh answer.

recall.prompt: On a cache miss, in what order does the resolver ask?
options: .com TLD server, then root server, then the station's nameserver
Root server, then .com TLD server, then the station's nameserver
The station's nameserver, then the root server
The old server, then the new server
recall.why: Each step points to the next: the root knows who runs .com, the .com servers know which nameserver holds the station's records, and that authoritative nameserver has the answer.

recall.prompt: It's Wednesday. Your team moves the company website to a new server on Friday at 6 PM. The A record's TTL is 86400. What do you do, and when?

keyIdeas.idea: Lower the TTL now, well before Friday
The old one-day copies must expire before the move
Keep the old server running after the move, then raise the TTL again

recall.model: Lower the TTL today, to around 300 seconds. Caches that already hold the record keep their one-day copy, so lowering it on Wednesday means every old copy has expired by Thursday evening, well before Friday's move. After the switch, the worst case is about 5 minutes of old answers. Keep the old server running for a few days for resolvers and programs that ignore the TTL, watch its traffic fall, and once the new server is solid, raise the TTL back to an hour or a day.

recall.prompt: A coworker says: "DNS changes take 24 to 48 hours to propagate, nothing we can do." What is actually happening, and what could they have done?

keyIdeas.idea: Nothing travels: cached copies are expiring
The wait is set by the TTL
Lowering the TTL ahead of time shortens the wait

recall.model: Nothing is travelling. The new answer was live the moment they saved it. What takes time is resolvers and devices around the world holding old copies until each copy's TTL runs out, so the wait is set by the TTL the record had before the change. If they had lowered it to a few minutes a day or two ahead, most of the world would have switched within minutes.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Marcus is moving our show archive, every old episode, to a new server this Thursday at 4 PM. The archive has its own name, archive.hollowpinefm.com, with a TTL of 86400. It's Monday night. His plan: lower the TTL to 60 seconds on Thursday morning, "to be safe," move at 4, and switch the old server off at 4:05. Ivy already asked if she should be worried.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Is Marcus's plan okay? What should the timeline be?

keyIdeas.idea: Thursday morning is too late: copies saved before then keep their one-day timer
Lower it now, at least a day before the move
Don't switch the old server off right away

coldCase.model: Thursday morning is too late. A resolver that fetched the old record at 8 AM Thursday got a one-day timer and keeps it until 8 AM Friday, long after the 4 PM move. Lower the TTL tonight, so every one-day copy has expired by Tuesday night and Thursday's move reaches nearly everyone within a minute. And don't switch the old server off at 4:05. Keep it serving for a few days for resolvers and programs that ignore the TTL, watch its visits drop to zero, then turn it off and raise the TTL again.
